topics.name: Stamp Act
topics.kicker: 1765 British tax on printed paper · “No taxation without representation”
topics.briefing: In 1765, Parliament ordered American colonists to use specially marked, taxed paper for newspapers, legal documents, pamphlets, and even playing cards, to help pay for British troops in America. The colonies exploded in protest: crowds hanged tax collectors in effigy, the Sons of Liberty organized, nine colonies sent delegates to a special congress, and merchants stopped buying British goods. Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 but passed the Declaratory Act the same day, insisting it could still make laws for the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.”
topics.answerHtml: Stamp Act of 1765 (accept Duties in American Colonies Act; prompt on stamp tax; do not accept “Sugar Act,” “Townshend Acts,” or “Tea Act”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: During a debate over this law, Isaac Barré [“bah-RAY”], a member of Parliament who had fought in the French and Indian War, defended the colonists by saying that British oppression, not British care, had planted them in America. The city of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, is named partly for him.
tossups.r: In that speech, Barré called the colonists “Sons of Liberty.” For 10 points, name this 1765 British tax on newspapers, legal papers, and playing cards.

tossups.p: On August 14, 1765, a Boston crowd hanged an effigy of Andrew Oliver from a large elm, later called the Liberty Tree, because he had been chosen to collect this law’s tax in Massachusetts. Oliver agreed to resign the next day, and less than two weeks later a mob wrecked the mansion of Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson.
tossups.r: Parliament repealed this law in 1766. For 10 points, name this tax that required colonists to buy specially marked paper.

tossups.p: In May 1765, a new member of Virginia’s House of Burgesses introduced resolutions declaring that only Virginia’s own assembly could tax Virginians. In a speech against this law, he reportedly warned that “Caesar had his Brutus” and that King George III might “profit by their example.”
tossups.r: That burgess was Patrick Henry. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on printed paper, which led to the cry “No taxation without representation.”

tossups.p: In October 1765, delegates from nine colonies met at New York’s City Hall to protest this law, and they approved a Declaration of Rights and Grievances written mostly by John Dickinson. That meeting took its name from this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1765 law, proposed by George Grenville, that taxed newspapers and legal documents.

tossups.p: People accused of breaking this law could be tried in vice-admiralty courts, which had no juries, and its tax had to be paid in British currency rather than colonial paper money. Prime Minister George Grenville proposed it to help pay for about 10,000 British soldiers kept in North America.
tossups.r: Colonists protested it with the slogan “No taxation without representation.” For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on printed paper.

tossups.p: In February 1766, Benjamin Franklin told the House of Commons that the colonists would never pay this law’s tax unless they were forced to by arms. William Pitt also urged Parliament to repeal it, telling members that he rejoiced that America had resisted.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tax that Parliament repealed in March 1766, the same day it passed the Declaratory Act.

tossups.p: On the same day in March 1766 that Parliament repealed this law, it passed an act declaring that it could make laws binding the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The government of the Marquess of Rockingham [“ROCK-ing-um”] carried out that repeal.
tossups.r: That act was the Declaratory Act. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax law, which sparked the cry “No taxation without representation.”

tossups.p: This law taxed dice and playing cards, along with diplomas, ship’s papers, almanacs, and pamphlets. It angered lawyers, printers, and merchants most of all, since their work used so much paper.
tossups.r: Newspapers and legal documents needed specially marked paper too. For 10 points, name this 1765 law proposed by George Grenville.

tossups.p: Merchants in New York, Philadelphia, and Boston agreed to stop importing British goods until this law was repealed, and British merchants who lost business then lobbied Parliament against it. Most of the officials chosen to distribute this law’s specially marked paper were pressured into resigning before it took effect on November 1, 1765.
tossups.r: Groups called the Sons of Liberty formed to fight it. For 10 points, name this 1765 British tax on printed paper.

tossups.p: Thomas Whately, a British official, defended this law by arguing that the colonists were “virtually represented” in Parliament even though they elected no members to it. In Massachusetts, John Adams wrote instructions for the town of Braintree protesting this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1765 law that colonists opposed with the cry “No taxation without representation.”

tossups.p: In Boston, a secret club of artisans and shopkeepers called the Loyal Nine organized the first protests against this law. A shoemaker named Ebenezer Mackintosh led the crowds that attacked the property of royal officials.
tossups.r: Groups called the Sons of Liberty soon formed in other colonies. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on printed paper, repealed in 1766.

tossups.p: One year after the Sugar Act lowered the tax on molasses but enforced it more strictly, Parliament passed this law, the first direct tax it ever placed on the American colonies. A Quartering Act passed soon afterward required colonies to supply British troops with housing and supplies.
tossups.r: Colonists protested this law by boycotting British goods. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on newspapers and legal documents.

tossups.p: Timothy Ruggles of Massachusetts presided over a congress that met to oppose this law, but he refused to sign its petitions, and his colony’s legislature later scolded him for it. James Otis had proposed calling that congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1765 British tax law, whose repeal came with the Declaratory Act.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin hurt his reputation at home by recommending his friend John Hughes to distribute this law’s specially marked paper in Pennsylvania. In September 1765, Franklin’s wife, Deborah, refused to leave their Philadelphia house and prepared to defend it when an angry crowd threatened it.
tossups.r: Franklin later testified against this law in Parliament. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on printed paper.

tossups.p: Grateful New Yorkers voted to put up statues of King George III and William Pitt after Parliament repealed this law. Years later, after the Declaration of Independence was read in the city in July 1776, a crowd pulled down the king’s statue at Bowling Green.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1765 British tax on newspapers, legal documents, and playing cards.

clues.t: Passed by Parliament in 1765 to raise money from the American colonies
Taxed printed paper, such as newspapers and legal documents
Protested with the cry “No taxation without representation”
Sons of Liberty groups formed to fight it
Proposed by Prime Minister George Grenville, who had also passed the Sugar Act (1764)
Repealed in March 1766, the same day Parliament passed the Declaratory Act, claiming power over the colonies “in all cases whatsoever”
Delegates from nine colonies met in New York (October 1765) and approved a Declaration of Rights and Grievances
Patrick Henry’s Virginia Resolves (May 1765); he reportedly warned that “Caesar had his Brutus”
Meant to help pay for about 10,000 British troops kept in America after the French and Indian (Seven Years’) War
Merchants boycotted British goods with nonimportation agreements
Boston crowds hanged an effigy of tax collector Andrew Oliver from the Liberty Tree (August 1765)
Benjamin Franklin told the House of Commons (1766) that colonists would never pay it unless forced
The first direct tax Parliament placed on the colonies
Isaac Barré called the colonists “Sons of Liberty” in a 1765 speech in Parliament; Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, is partly named for him
A mob wrecked Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson’s Boston mansion (August 26, 1765)
John Dickinson wrote most of the Declaration of Rights and Grievances; the congress met at New York’s City Hall
Accused violators faced vice-admiralty courts without juries; the tax had to be paid in British currency, not colonial paper money
William Pitt said he rejoiced that America had resisted; the Marquess of Rockingham’s government repealed it
Also taxed dice, playing cards, diplomas, almanacs, pamphlets, and ship’s papers
Under pressure, most of the chosen tax distributors resigned before it took effect on November 1, 1765
Thomas Whately argued colonists were “virtually represented” in Parliament; John Adams wrote the Braintree Instructions against it
Boston’s Loyal Nine organized the first protests; shoemaker Ebenezer Mackintosh led the crowds
Timothy Ruggles presided over the 1765 congress but refused to sign; James Otis had proposed it
Franklin’s friend John Hughes was named a distributor; Deborah Franklin defended their Philadelphia house (1765)
Grateful New Yorkers voted for statues of George III and William Pitt; the king’s statue at Bowling Green was pulled down in 1776
A Quartering Act (1765), passed soon after, required colonies to house and supply British troops

trap.title: Which British tax?
trap.body: Parliament taxed the colonies several times before the Revolution. The Sugar Act (1764) taxed molasses, the Stamp Act (1765) taxed printed paper, the Townshend Acts (1767) taxed glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea brought into the colonies, and the Tea Act (1773) led to the Boston Tea Party. The Stamp Act Congress is its own answer line, so answering with the law when a question asks for “this meeting” or “this congress” is wrong.
trap.fix: Grenville, 1765, newspapers, playing cards, Andrew Oliver, Patrick Henry’s Virginia Resolves, and repeal alongside the Declaratory Act mean the Stamp Act. Molasses and 1764 mean the Sugar Act; glass, paint, and Charles Townshend mean the Townshend Acts.
trap.line: Real answer line: Stamp Act of 1765 (accept Duties in American Colonies Act; prompt on stamp tax; do not accept “Sugar Act,” “Townshend Acts,” or “Tea Act”)

topics.name: Seminoles
topics.kicker: Native nation of Florida · Fought three wars against the United States
topics.briefing: In the 1700s, Creek families and other Native people moved into Spanish Florida and formed a new nation, the Seminoles, who were allied with communities of Black people who had escaped slavery. They fought three wars against the United States, and the longest, in which Osceola was a famous war leader, lasted from 1835 to 1842. Most Seminoles were forced west to Indian Territory, but a few hundred stayed in the Everglades, and their descendants still live in Florida.
topics.answerHtml: Seminoles (or Seminole Nation; accept Seminole Tribe of Florida; prompt on Miccosukee, Black Seminoles, or Five Civilized Tribes; do not accept “Cherokee” or “Creek”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This people’s name is often traced to the Spanish word cimarrón [“see-mah-ROHN”], meaning “wild” or “runaway,” because their ancestors broke away from other nations and moved into Spanish lands. Many of those ancestors were Creek people from Georgia and Alabama who moved south in the 1700s.
tossups.r: Osceola was one of their most famous war leaders. For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida.

tossups.p: In 1818, a U.S. general who had invaded Spanish Florida to fight this people captured St. Marks and Pensacola and executed two British subjects, Alexander Arbuthnot [“ar-BUTH-not”] and Robert Ambrister, whom he accused of helping them. The next year, Spain agreed to give Florida to the United States.
tossups.r: That general was Andrew Jackson. For 10 points, name this Native nation that fought three wars against the United States in Florida.

tossups.p: On December 28, 1835, warriors of this nation ambushed Major Francis Dade’s column of about 110 soldiers, and only a few soldiers survived. On the same day, a war leader of this nation killed the Indian agent Wiley Thompson outside Fort King.
tossups.r: That leader was Osceola. Those attacks began the second of three wars between this nation and the United States. For 10 points, name this nation of Florida.

tossups.p: In 1837, soldiers acting on General Thomas Jesup’s orders seized a war leader of this nation when he came to talk under a white flag of truce, and many Americans condemned the act. That leader, whose portrait was painted by George Catlin, died a few months later at Fort Moultrie in South Carolina.
tossups.r: That leader was Osceola. For 10 points, name this Native nation that fought the United States in Florida in the 1800s.

tossups.p: Under the 1823 Treaty of Moultrie Creek, this nation moved onto an inland reservation, but a later treaty signed at Payne’s Landing in 1832 called for its people to move west of the Mississippi River. Many of them said the leaders who signed that second treaty had no right to do so.
tossups.r: The dispute led to a long war. For 10 points, name this nation that resisted removal in Florida, led partly by Osceola.

tossups.p: John Horse, also called Juan Caballo [“HWAHN kah-BAH-yoh”], was a leader of this nation’s Black allies, many of whom had escaped slavery in Georgia and the Carolinas. In 1849 and 1850, he and the leader Wild Cat led a group of this nation’s people and their Black allies to northern Mexico.
tossups.r: Osceola fought for this nation in the 1830s. For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida.

tossups.p: On Christmas Day 1837, Colonel Zachary Taylor’s army fought warriors of this nation at the Battle of Lake Okeechobee [“oh-kee-CHOH-bee”], one of the largest battles of a seven-year war. Leaders on the other side included Alligator and Abiaka [“ah-bee-AH-kah”], a medicine man also called Sam Jones.
tossups.r: Taylor later became president. For 10 points, name this nation of Florida, whose war leaders included Osceola.

tossups.p: The medicine man Abiaka [“ah-bee-AH-kah”], also called Sam Jones, never surrendered and led his followers deep into the Everglades, where soldiers could not catch them. This nation’s tribe there calls itself “unconquered,” and it is often said that it never signed a peace treaty with the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida, which fought three wars against the United States.

tossups.p: In 1858, Billy Bowlegs, also known as Holata Micco [“hoh-LAH-tah MIK-oh”], agreed to move west with many of his followers, ending the last of three wars between his nation and the United States. That war had begun in 1855, after army surveyors damaged crops belonging to his band.
tossups.r: A few hundred of his people stayed in the Everglades. For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida, whose war leaders included Osceola.

tossups.p: In November 1837, the war leader Wild Cat, also called Coacoochee [“koh-uh-KOO-chee”], and other prisoners from this nation squeezed through a narrow opening high in a wall of Fort Marion in St. Augustine and escaped. A more famous leader of this nation, who was held in the same fort, did not go with them.
tossups.r: That leader was Osceola. For 10 points, name this Native nation that resisted removal in the 1830s.

tossups.p: After their removal west, this nation’s people were at first made to settle on Creek land, but in 1856 they received a separate reservation of their own. Their nation’s capital in Oklahoma is Wewoka [“wee-WOH-kuh”].
tossups.r: Others stayed in Florida. For 10 points, name this nation, one of the “Five Civilized Tribes,” that was once led in war by Osceola.

tossups.p: In 2007, a tribe of this nation bought the Hard Rock Cafe company, a deal often described as the first purchase of a major international company by a Native American tribe. The separate Miccosukee [“mik-uh-SOO-kee”] Tribe, whose members share much of this nation’s history, was recognized by the U.S. government in 1962.
tossups.r: Florida State University’s teams use this nation’s name, with the tribe’s approval. For 10 points, name this Native nation, which fought three wars against the United States.

tossups.p: Members of this nation are known for colorful patchwork clothing sewn from narrow strips of cloth, and for chickees [“CHICK-eez”], open-sided houses with roofs thatched with palmetto leaves. Many of its people speak Mikasuki [“mih-KAH-soo-kee”] or the Muscogee language.
tossups.r: Their 1830s war leaders included Osceola. For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida.

tossups.p: In 1816, U.S. forces destroyed a fort on the Apalachicola [“ap-uh-lach-ih-KOH-luh”] River that had been held by Black people who had escaped slavery, along with some Native allies. That attack, and clashes over the next year, helped lead to the first of three wars between this nation and the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Native nation, later led in war by Osceola, that lived in Florida.

tossups.p: Generals including Winfield Scott and Thomas Jesup commanded U.S. forces against this nation in a war from 1835 to 1842, often called the longest and costliest war the United States ever fought against a Native nation. That war followed the Indian Removal Act of 1830.
tossups.r: Osceola led many of its warriors. For 10 points, name this Native nation that resisted removal from Florida.

clues.t: Native nation of Florida, formed in the 1700s mostly by Creek people who moved south
Osceola was a famous war leader in their fight against removal
Fought three wars against the United States (1817–1818, 1835–1842, 1855–1858)
Most were forced west to Indian Territory (Oklahoma); one of the “Five Civilized Tribes”
Andrew Jackson invaded Spanish Florida in the first war (1818), capturing St. Marks and Pensacola
Jackson executed two Britons, Alexander Arbuthnot and Robert Ambrister, accusing them of helping this people
Soon after, Spain gave Florida to the United States in the Adams–Onís Treaty (1819)
The second war began when they attacked Major Francis Dade’s soldiers (December 28, 1835)
Allied with Black communities of people who had escaped slavery; John Horse was a leader
Osceola was seized under a flag of truce (1837) on General Thomas Jesup’s orders and died at Fort Moultrie (1838)
A few hundred stayed hidden in the Everglades; their Florida tribe calls itself “unconquered”
Zachary Taylor fought them at the Battle of Lake Okeechobee (Christmas Day 1837)
The Treaty of Payne’s Landing (1832) called for their removal west; many of them rejected it
Florida State University’s teams use their name, with the Florida tribe’s approval
Their name is often traced to the Spanish word cimarrón, meaning “wild” or “runaway”
The Treaty of Moultrie Creek (1823) moved them onto an inland reservation
Osceola killed Indian agent Wiley Thompson outside Fort King on the day of Dade’s battle
George Catlin painted Osceola’s portrait at Fort Moultrie shortly before he died
Wild Cat (Coacoochee) and other prisoners escaped from Fort Marion in St. Augustine (1837)
John Horse and Wild Cat led a group to northern Mexico (1849–1850)
The medicine man Abiaka (Sam Jones) never surrendered
Billy Bowlegs (Holata Micco) agreed to move west in 1858, ending the third war
In the West they were first placed on Creek land; in 1856 they got their own reservation, and their capital is Wewoka, Oklahoma
Their Florida tribe bought the Hard Rock Cafe company (2007); the separate Miccosukee Tribe was recognized in 1962
Known for colorful patchwork clothing and chickees, open-sided houses thatched with palmetto leaves
In 1816, U.S. forces destroyed a fort on the Apalachicola River held by people who had escaped slavery, a step toward the first war
The 1835–1842 war is often called the longest and costliest U.S. war against a Native nation; Winfield Scott and Thomas Jesup commanded in it

trap.title: Which Southeastern nation?
trap.body: The Seminole, Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, and Chickasaw were all called the “Five Civilized Tribes,” and all were forced west in the 1800s, so their clues blur together. The Seminoles grew partly out of the Creek, but answering “Creek” or “Cherokee” is wrong when the clues point to Florida. The three wars are separate answer lines, so naming the people when a question asks for “this war” loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Florida, the Everglades, Osceola, Dade’s battle, Billy Bowlegs, and Andrew Jackson’s 1818 invasion mean the Seminoles. Sequoyah, John Ross, and New Echota mean the Cherokee; the Red Sticks and Horseshoe Bend mean the Creek. Listen for “this nation” versus “this war.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Seminoles (or Seminole Nation; accept Seminole Tribe of Florida; prompt on Miccosukee, Black Seminoles, or Five Civilized Tribes; do not accept “Cherokee” or “Creek”)

topics.name: Shays’ Rebellion
topics.kicker: Massachusetts farmers’ revolt, 1786–1787 · Exposed the Articles’ weakness
topics.briefing: In 1786, farmers in western Massachusetts were losing their land, and some were even jailed, because they could not pay their debts and the state’s heavy taxes, which had to be paid in gold or silver. Led partly by Daniel Shays, a veteran of the Revolution, they shut down courts and in January 1787 marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield, where militia cannons drove them off. The uprising scared many leaders into pushing for a stronger national government at the Constitutional Convention that summer.
topics.answerHtml: Shays’ Rebellion (or Shays’s Rebellion; prompt on Shays; do not accept “Whiskey Rebellion”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Rebels in this uprising wore sprigs of hemlock in their hats and called themselves “Regulators,” and many of them were veterans of the Revolutionary War. They began by closing county courts in towns such as Northampton to stop judges from taking farms for unpaid debts.
tossups.r: Its best-known leader was a former army captain from Pelham. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts revolt of 1786 and 1787 led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: Writing from Paris, Thomas Jefferson responded to this uprising by telling James Madison that “a little rebellion now and then is a good thing.” Abigail Adams, writing from London, took a harsher view, calling its participants “ignorant, restless desperadoes.”
tossups.r: This revolt pushed many leaders to support a stronger national government. For 10 points, name this uprising led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: A message from Luke Day saying that his men would attack a day late was intercepted, so the main force of this uprising marched without them. On January 25, 1787, General William Shepard’s militia fired cannons at that force near the federal arsenal at Springfield, killing four men.
tossups.r: That defeat was the turning point of this uprising. For 10 points, name this revolt of Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: After an overnight march through a snowstorm, General Benjamin Lincoln’s army surprised and scattered the main force of this uprising at Petersham in February 1787. Lincoln’s army had been paid for by wealthy Boston merchants, because the national government could not afford to raise troops.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rebellion, led by Daniel Shays, that showed the weakness of the Articles of Confederation.

tossups.p: Before this uprising, a state government raised taxes sharply to pay off its war debts and required that they be paid in gold or silver coin, which few farmers in the state’s western hills had. Farmers who could not pay lost their land in court or were sent to debtors’ prison.
tossups.r: Governor James Bowdoin [“BOH-din”] sent the militia to stop it. For 10 points, name this 1786–1787 rebellion of Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: Henry Knox, the national Secretary at War, sent George Washington an alarming report claiming that the rebels in this uprising wanted all property to be shared in common. Fear of this uprising helped persuade Washington to come out of retirement and travel to Philadelphia in 1787.
tossups.r: It was put down by state militia in early 1787. For 10 points, name this revolt of Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: After this uprising, voters replaced Governor James Bowdoin [“BOH-din”] with John Hancock, who had held the office before and who pardoned many of its participants. Hancock’s government also lowered taxes and gave some relief to people in debt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this revolt of Massachusetts farmers in 1786 and 1787, led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: In September 1786, the Annapolis Convention called for a meeting the next year to fix the national government, and news of this uprising over the following months convinced more states to send delegates. The Confederation Congress could not raise an army to stop it.
tossups.r: The Massachusetts militia ended it in 1787. For 10 points, name this revolt of indebted farmers led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: In a letter to James Madison, George Washington asked, “What stronger evidence can be given of the want of energy in our governments than these disorders?” Washington was writing about this uprising, in which armed crowds forced courts to close in the fall of 1786.
tossups.r: Its rebels were mostly farmers from western Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this rebellion led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: During this uprising, the state legislature passed a Riot Act and suspended the writ of habeas corpus [“HAY-bee-us KOR-pus”] so that suspected leaders could be held without trial. One of those leaders, Job Shattuck, was captured in late 1786.
tossups.r: Its best-known leader was Daniel Shays. For 10 points, name this 1786–1787 uprising in Massachusetts.

tossups.p: After this uprising collapsed in February 1787, its best-known leader fled to Vermont, which was then an independent republic outside the United States. A last clash came that month at Sheffield, in the far southwestern corner of the state where the uprising began.
tossups.r: That leader was Daniel Shays. For 10 points, name this rebellion of indebted farmers in western Massachusetts.

tossups.p: Partly in response to this uprising, the U.S. Constitution lets Congress call out the militia to “suppress Insurrections” and promises federal protection to the states against “domestic Violence.” Under the old system, Congress had no power to collect taxes or raise troops on its own to stop it.
tossups.r: The state militia ended it in early 1787. For 10 points, name this 1786–1787 revolt in western Massachusetts led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: Unlike the later Whiskey Rebellion, this uprising was put down by state militia rather than a national army, since the Confederation Congress could not raise one. Its leaders had asked for paper money and for laws that would delay the collection of debts.
tossups.r: It had begun in 1786 when farmers closed courts in western Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this rebellion led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: The leader of this uprising had risen to the rank of captain in the Continental Army during the Revolution, and like many of his followers, he came home deep in debt. He lived in the hill town of Pelham, east of the Connecticut River.
tossups.r: That captain was Daniel Shays. For 10 points, name the uprising that he led in western Massachusetts in 1786 and 1787.

tossups.p: Merchants in Boston who owed money to British lenders demanded hard money from country storekeepers, who in turn sued farmers, setting off the debt crisis behind this uprising. Western farmers also resented a state legislature that they saw as run by eastern merchants.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1786–1787 revolt led by Daniel Shays, which helped lead to the Constitutional Convention.

clues.t: A revolt of indebted farmers in western Massachusetts (1786–1787)
Its best-known leader, Daniel Shays, was a former Continental Army captain from Pelham
Showed the weakness of the national government under the Articles of Confederation
Pushed leaders toward a stronger government at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia (1787)
January 25, 1787: rebels marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield; William Shepard’s militia fired cannons, killing four
General Benjamin Lincoln’s militia, paid for by Boston merchants, scattered the rebels at Petersham (February 1787)
Thomas Jefferson, in Paris, wrote to James Madison that “a little rebellion now and then is a good thing”
Causes: heavy state taxes and debts that had to be paid in hard money (gold or silver coin)
Rebels calling themselves “Regulators” closed county courts to stop farms from being taken for debt (1786)
Voters replaced Governor James Bowdoin with John Hancock, who pardoned many rebels
Unlike the Whiskey Rebellion (1794), it was ended by state militia, not a national army
Fear of it helped draw George Washington out of retirement to attend the convention in Philadelphia
Rebels wore sprigs of hemlock in their hats
Luke Day’s message delaying his attack was intercepted, so the main rebel force marched on Springfield without his men
Henry Knox, the Secretary at War, warned Washington that the rebels wanted all property shared in common
Abigail Adams, in London, called the rebels “ignorant, restless desperadoes”
Washington to Madison: “What stronger evidence can be given of the want of energy in our governments than these disorders?”
The state passed a Riot Act and suspended habeas corpus; leader Job Shattuck was captured in late 1786
Shays fled to Vermont, then an independent republic, and was pardoned in 1788; a last clash came at Sheffield (February 1787)
Crowds first closed the court at Northampton (August 1786)
The Annapolis Convention (September 1786) had already called for a meeting the next year; the uprising convinced more states to attend
The Constitution lets Congress call out the militia to “suppress Insurrections” and protects states against “domestic Violence”
Boston merchants owed British lenders and demanded hard money from country storekeepers, who sued farmers
The rebels wanted paper money and laws delaying debt collection; afterward the state lowered taxes and gave debtors some relief

trap.title: Shays’ or Whiskey?
trap.body: Two early farmers’ revolts against taxes are easy to mix up. Shays’ Rebellion (1786–1787) was in western Massachusetts under the Articles of Confederation and was ended by state militia; the Whiskey Rebellion (1791–1794) was in western Pennsylvania against Alexander Hamilton’s tax on whiskey and ended when George Washington sent a federal army. Saying only “Shays” earns a prompt, since Daniel Shays is a person, not an event.
trap.fix: Massachusetts, Springfield, Benjamin Lincoln, hemlock sprigs, and the Articles of Confederation mean Shays’; Pittsburgh, stills, Hamilton’s excise tax, and Washington’s militia army mean Whiskey; John Fries and a tax on houses mean Fries’s Rebellion (1799).
trap.line: Real answer line: Shays’ Rebellion (or Shays’s Rebellion; prompt on Shays; do not accept “Whiskey Rebellion”)

topics.name: Sitting Bull
topics.kicker: Hunkpapa Lakota holy man and leader · Led resistance on the northern Plains
topics.briefing: Sitting Bull was a Hunkpapa Lakota holy man and leader who refused to give up his people’s land on the northern Plains. Weeks before the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876, he had a vision of soldiers falling into the Lakota camp, and the Lakota and Cheyenne then defeated George Armstrong Custer’s 7th Cavalry. He later spent four years in Canada, toured with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West, and was killed in 1890 when Indian police tried to arrest him at Standing Rock.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: During a Sun Dance in June 1876, this holy man had a vision of soldiers falling upside down into his people’s camp like grasshoppers, a sign of a coming victory. Days later, Lakota and Cheyenne warriors led by Crazy Horse fought General George Crook’s army to a standstill at the Rosebud.
tossups.r: Later that month, this man’s followers helped defeat George Armstrong Custer at the Little Bighorn. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader.

tossups.p: In July 1881, this man surrendered at Fort Buford in Dakota Territory, where his young son Crow Foot handed over his father’s rifle. He had returned from four years in Canada after hunger and the disappearance of the buffalo left his followers struggling to survive.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader whose people had defeated George Custer at the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: In 1885, the Montreal studio of photographer William Notman took a portrait of this man standing beside a famous showman, later captioned “Foes in ’76, Friends in ’85.” That summer, this man toured for about four months with the showman’s traveling company.
tossups.r: That showman was Buffalo Bill Cody. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who nicknamed Annie Oakley “Little Sure Shot.”

tossups.p: Lieutenant Bull Head and Sergeant Red Tomahawk led a group of Indian agency police to this man’s cabin on the Grand River before dawn one December morning. Agent James McLaughlin had sent them because he feared this man would lead a new religious movement among his people.
tossups.r: This man was killed during that arrest attempt on December 15, 1890. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader.

tossups.p: As a boy, this man was nicknamed “Slow” because he was so careful and deliberate. At about age 14, he counted coup on a Crow warrior, and his proud father then gave his own name to his son.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota holy man who led his people at the time of the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: Unlike Red Cloud, this leader refused to sign the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, and he kept his followers off the reservations, hunting buffalo on the northern Plains. After gold was found in the Black Hills, the U.S. ordered all Lakota bands onto reservations by January 31, 1876.
tossups.r: This man’s refusal led to the war in which Custer was defeated. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader.

tossups.p: After seeing her shoot in St. Paul, Minnesota, in 1884, this man adopted a young sharpshooter from Ohio as an honorary daughter and gave her a Lakota name. The next year, both of them performed with the same traveling show.
tossups.r: That sharpshooter, Annie Oakley, became known by his nickname for her, “Little Sure Shot.” For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader.

tossups.p: After his surrender, this man was held as a prisoner of war at Fort Randall for nearly two years. In 1883, he was allowed to rejoin his people at an agency along the Missouri River, and he settled on a farm near the Grand River.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who had fled to Canada after the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: In 1864, this man fought against General Alfred Sully’s army at the Battle of Killdeer Mountain in Dakota Territory. He went on to become the most important leader of the Lakota bands that refused to live on reservations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who led the great camp at the Little Bighorn in 1876.

tossups.p: In 1889, this man tried to stop his people from signing an agreement that broke the Great Sioux Reservation into six smaller reservations and opened millions of acres to white settlers. Most Lakota men signed anyway, after long pressure from a commission led by General George Crook.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who toured with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West in 1885.

tossups.p: The Lakota call a famous battle fought beside this man’s camp “the Greasy Grass,” after their name for the river there. His huge camp beside that river in Montana Territory included Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho people.
tossups.r: Americans call that 1876 battle the Little Bighorn, where Custer died. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota holy man.

tossups.p: This man and his followers called Canada the “Grandmother’s Land,” after Queen Victoria, and there he befriended James Walsh, an officer of the North-West Mounted Police, near Wood Mountain. Canada’s government refused to give his people a reservation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who fled north after the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: In 1890, this man allowed Kicking Bear to teach a new religious movement at his camp, though historians still debate how strongly he believed in it. That movement had begun with the Paiute prophet Wovoka [“woh-VOH-kuh”].
tossups.r: Officials feared his role in that movement, the Ghost Dance, and sent police to arrest him. For 10 points, name this Lakota leader killed in December 1890.

tossups.p: At the start of a June 1876 battle, Major Marcus Reno’s soldiers charged the camp circle of this man’s own band at the southern end of the village, but warriors including Gall drove them back across the river and onto the bluffs.
tossups.r: Later that day, Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated George Armstrong Custer. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa holy man whose vision foretold that victory.

tossups.p: In 1953, some of this man’s relatives moved what they said were his remains from Fort Yates, North Dakota, to a hill near Mobridge, South Dakota. A granite bust of him there was carved by Korczak Ziolkowski [“KOR-chak jool-KOFF-skee”], the sculptor of the Crazy Horse Memorial.
tossups.r: He had been killed in 1890 during an attempt to arrest him. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader, who toured with Buffalo Bill in 1885.

clues.t: Hunkpapa Lakota (Sioux) holy man and leader on the northern Plains (c. 1831–1890)
Led the great camp whose warriors defeated Custer at the Little Bighorn (June 25–26, 1876)
Toured with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West in 1885
Killed on December 15, 1890, when Indian police tried to arrest him at Standing Rock
At a Sun Dance in June 1876, he had a vision of soldiers falling upside down into the Lakota camp
Led his followers into Canada after the Little Bighorn (1877–1881)
Surrendered at Fort Buford in July 1881; his young son Crow Foot handed over his rifle
Adopted Annie Oakley as an honorary daughter (1884) and nicknamed her “Little Sure Shot”
Agent James McLaughlin feared he would lead the Ghost Dance and ordered his arrest
His death came two weeks before the Wounded Knee massacre (December 29, 1890)
Refused to sign the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, unlike Red Cloud
Allied with the Oglala war leader Crazy Horse, who fought General George Crook at the Rosebud days after the Sun Dance
Nicknamed “Slow” as a boy; took his father’s name after counting coup on a Crow warrior at about 14
William Notman’s studio in Montreal photographed him with Buffalo Bill (1885): “Foes in ’76, Friends in ’85”
Lieutenant Bull Head and Sergeant Red Tomahawk led the police sent to arrest him at his cabin on the Grand River
In Canada, the “Grandmother’s Land,” he befriended James Walsh of the North-West Mounted Police near Wood Mountain
Held as a prisoner of war at Fort Randall (1881–1883) before moving to the Standing Rock Agency
Fought General Alfred Sully’s army at Killdeer Mountain (1864)
Opposed the 1889 agreement, pushed by George Crook’s commission, that split the Great Sioux Reservation into six smaller ones
The Lakota call the Little Bighorn the Battle of the Greasy Grass
Let Kicking Bear teach the Ghost Dance at his camp (1890); the movement began with the Paiute prophet Wovoka
At the Little Bighorn, Major Marcus Reno attacked his band’s camp first, and warriors including Gall drove Reno back
First buried at Fort Yates; in 1953 relatives moved what they said were his remains near Mobridge, where Korczak Ziolkowski carved a bust

trap.title: Which Lakota leader?
trap.body: Several famous Lakota leaders appear in the same tossups. Sitting Bull was a Hunkpapa holy man whose vision foretold the victory at the Little Bighorn; Crazy Horse was an Oglala war leader who led warriors in the fighting there; and Red Cloud was an Oglala chief who signed the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie. Geronimo (Apache) and Chief Joseph (Nez Perce) led resistance in other regions.
trap.fix: Canada, Fort Buford, Buffalo Bill’s Wild West, “Little Sure Shot,” and the arrest at Standing Rock in 1890 mean Sitting Bull. The Rosebud, a surrender at Camp Robinson in 1877, and the unfinished mountain carving in South Dakota mean Crazy Horse.
